result.topic_en: An argument about highly composite numbers N written as products of primorial-type factors e^{θ(p_1)+θ(p_2)+...}: it compares d(N) with d(N') for a modified number N' and derives inequalities relating log p_1 and log p_r.
result.transcription:
N is \underline{highly composite}
$N = e^{\vartheta(p_1)+\vartheta(p_2)+\vartheta(p_3)+\cdots\cdots}$
$d(N) = 2^{\pi(p_1)}\,(\tfrac{3}{2})^{\pi(p_2)}\,(\tfrac{4}{3})^{\pi(p_3)}\cdots\cdots$
Let $N' = N e^{\vartheta(q_1)+\vartheta(q_r)-\vartheta(p_1)-\vartheta(p_r)}$
Then $d(N') \geq d(N).\,2^{\pi(q_1)-\pi(p_1)}.\,(1+\frac{1}{r})^{\pi(q_r)-\pi(p_r)}$
First let us suppose that $q_1 > p_1$, $q_r < p_r$ and
$\pi(q_1) = \pi(p_1) + n$
$\pi(q_r) = \pi(p_r) - \left[\frac{n\log 2}{\log(1+\frac{1}{r})}\right]$
Then we have $d(N') \geq d(N)$ and so $N' \geq N$. That is to say
$\vartheta(q_1)+\vartheta(q_r) \geq \vartheta(p_1)+\vartheta(p_r)$.
But if $\alpha > \beta$, it is easy to see that
$\{\pi(\alpha)-\pi(\beta)\}\log\alpha \geq \vartheta(\alpha)-\vartheta(\beta) \geq \{\pi(\alpha)-\pi(\beta)\}\log\beta$.
Hence $\{\pi(q_1)-\pi(p_1)\}\log q_1 \geq \{\pi(p_r)-\pi(q_r)\}\log q_r$,
or $n\log q_1 \geq \left[\frac{n\log 2}{\log(1+\frac{1}{r})}\right]\log q_r$.
But it is [-easy-] to show that, if $\pi(\alpha) = \pi(\beta) + x$ and $x = o(\frac{\beta}{\log\beta})$, then
$\log\alpha = \log\beta + O(1)$.
Hence $\log q_1 = \log p_1 + O(1)$, $\log q_r = \log p_r + O(1)$,
and so $n\{\log p_1 + O(1)\} \geq \left[\frac{n\log 2}{\log(1+\frac{1}{r})}\right]\{\log p_r + O(1)\}$,
or $\log p_1 + O(1) \geq \left\{\frac{\log 2}{\log(1+\frac{1}{r})} + O(\frac{1}{n})\right\}\{\log p_r + O(1)\}$.
In other words $\frac{\log p_1}{\log 2} - \frac{\log p_r}{\log(1+\frac{1}{r})} \geq O\left(r + \frac{\log p_r}{n}\right)$.
Now we can choose $n$ so that $\log p_r = O(nr)$. Hence

Divisor function of such N as product of ratios to powers of prime-counting values
Comparison with modified number N' (exchange argument for highly composite numbers)
Bounds for difference of theta function via difference of pi
Small change in pi implies bounded change in log
